en: A Petition Submitted with the Catalogue of Items Brought Back by the Monk Chōkō:
The monk Chōkō, who was dispatched on an imperial mission to study the Dharma in Tang China, states:
In the fifth month of the third year of the Jōwa era, I set out on my long journey beyond ten thousand *li*. That year, I encountered turbulent winds and drifted about. (4)
In that year, he was likewise unable to cross the sea.
On the sixth month of the fifth year, he set forth.
On the eighth month of the same year, he arrived at Guangling Pavilion in Huainan City and took up residence there.
In the first month of winter, the envoys entered the capital for court;
Chang Xiao was unable to accompany the envoys to the city and remained alone in the guest house.
Many days passed in vain,
and as the year drew to a close, no imperial decree had yet arrived; consequently,
he traveled throughout the prefecture to seek out and rely upon a teacher.
Fortunately, I encountered the Abbot Wenxue, a consecration Ācārya at Qiling Temple,
as well as the Great Virtuous Yuanzhao, the Preceptor of the Three Teachings at Hualin Temple.
The Venerable Wenbo was a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra and,
moreover, a successor in the Dharma transmission of the Acharya Huiying.
He possessed a profound mastery of the sutras, vinayas, and the esoteric treasury.
The main pillar of the Dharma;
that to which the nation turns.
In the same year’s twelfth lunar month.
He requested that the Military Governor issue a formal decree,
assigning him to reside at Xiling Temple with the Venerable Wenxu as his preceptor.
He began his studies of the ritual protocols and also went to Huālín Monastery to inquire about the fundamental tenets of his own school from the Dharma Master Yuánzhào.
I have also obtained the written documents.
Yet, the Great Master still laments the cycle of transmigration within the Buddha-dharma and sighs for the deliverance of the common people from their suffering.
He bestowed upon me the Great Dharma of Vajra and granted me the rank of Ācārya.
Whether I have understood it or not, I prostrate with my knees.
Whether I am able to touch his feet or not,
I rely upon the great grace of the State and the compassion of the Great Master to study the Yoga of the Vajra Ocean.
I have practiced the secret dharma of the Great General.
This dharma is the very heart and mind of the Tathāgata,
and the parents of all sentient beings.
Within the moats of the capital city and within the sinews and veins of human beings,
he is the Great General.
Within the capital, it was not transmitted beyond the ten imperial attendants;
throughout the provinces, it did not emerge from the residences of the regional commanders.
This was to manifest that its spiritual efficacy was inconceivable.
Although the images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajra-devas, and others have long been present before us,
these specific images have never before been invited here.
Now, the Great General’s various bodily maṇḍalas, along with the essential ritual documents for the various numinous images, have been invited and brought into our sight.
Although it is said that the waves were fierce and surging,
and that the Silla rebels were in revolt,
he overcame those perils and reached the sacred realm in safety.
This is indeed what can be accomplished through the power of the Sage.
We humbly observe that Your Majesty, the Emperor,
possesses virtue as boundless as Heaven.
The Buddha-sun rises ever higher;
he is the father of humanity.
In his transformation of beings, the Buddha feels compassion for all living creatures and wets his feet with their welfare.
Assisting the Buddha in his entrustment, he has spread the Dharma-garment;
may Your Majesty’s compassionate nurturing serve as a model.
May the auspicious and numinous teachings of the Sage be hoped for from afar, newly arriving here.
It is like a tally and its seal;
were it not for a sage, who could fathom it?
This was the original view of Changxiao.
For thirty years, he traveled through the Han territories seeking the Buddha-dharma; having come here,
he has served to protect the state.
However, as the Tang Dynasty did not permit me to remain,
I returned with the mission.
I privately reflect that I first sought to bring these teachings here because they had arisen within this Dharma tradition.
Unable to bear the extreme of alternating joy and fear,
I respectfully entrust this memorial to the assistant judge, Fujiwara no Tadamoto,
for presentation to Your Majesty.
I have also requested a copy of the catalog of the *Famen* (Dharma Gate) and other texts, which I now respectfully present.
For having thus lightly troubled Your Majesty’s august presence, I am filled with trepidation and awe.
I, Chang Xiao, speak these words with utmost sincerity and profound reverence.
A Memorial Submitted by the Śramaṇa Chōkō, Dharma Master of the Great Dharma-Transmission, Who Entered Tang China to Study the Dharma, on the Second Day of the Ninth Month in the Sixth Year of Jōwa.
The Śramaṇa Chōkō, who entered Tang China to study the Dharma, respectfully states:

Regarding the Dharma-gates, Buddha images, and ritual implements newly requested from the capital: *Commentary on the Śata-śāstra* (1 volume, 3 fascicles), composed by Master Yuankang; *A Key to the Profundities of the Three Treatises* (1 volume, 2 fascicles), composed by Master Yuankang; *Exegesis on the Thirty-six Gates of the Madhyamaka-śāstra* (1 volume), composed by Master Yuankang; *Abbreviated Record of the Commentary on the Śata-śāstra* (1 volume, 2 fascicles), composed by Master Yichi; *Commentary on the Mahābuddhotpāda-sūtra* (1 volume, 6 fascicles), composed by Master Hongkang; *Profound Praise of the Mahābuddhotpāda-sūtra* (1 volume, 3 fascicles), composed by Master Weiqiao. The above comprises six works.
In response to the request submitted by the Master Xuetou and others of the Sanlun school,
it is generally held that what is spoken by the Buddha is called a *sūtra*,
while what is spoken by a Bodhisattva is called a *śāstra*.
Human teachers have composed works such as commentaries, chapter-by-chapter expositions, and biographies. Why is this?
It is because the sutras spoken by the Buddha alone are difficult for those of dull faculties to understand.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva composed this treatise to explain it;
even those of the most dull faculties have not yet grasped its essential meaning.
Consequently, various masters composed commentaries, chapters, and other works,
elaborating in detail upon the extensive purports of the sūtras and śāstras;
there were several such masters of these commentaries.
It is simply that the heterodox and the orthodox differ;
as for these various commentaries and treatises now presented,
they explain the sutras and śāstras with even greater subtlety.
The principles and meanings are extremely subtle and fine;
though these names exist in this land, their reality has not yet been fully transmitted.
This is what causes doubt and stagnation among the various students.
Now, the *Śata-śāstra* is the ford and path to the True Truth (*satya*).
Previously, I used the commentary of Jiaxiang Temple to explain the meaning of the text;
there were some points that were insufficient.
Now, I shall use the commentary of Master Yuankang to establish the definitive principles.
Furthermore, regarding the two schools of Emptiness and Existence as they debate the principle of true nature,
the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* serves as their fundamental model.
Although the original scripture arrived earlier, [the subsequent traditions developed based upon it].
The commentary on this has not yet been produced,
making it difficult to resolve its meaning.
For now, I shall employ this to rectify the points of contention between the two schools of Emptiness and Existence.
Now, if one wing were missing,
how could one fly through the void?
How much more so regarding the profound principle of the One Vehicle!
The meaning contradicts the text;
without relying on commentaries and records, it remains obscure and unmanifest.
Though one may labor to load it onto a carriage, [the essence is not conveyed].
I hope that by means of this, it may serve as a supplement to the sacred scriptures.

*The Commentary on the Karmavācanā of the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (1 volume, 4 fascicles), composed by Vinaya Master Daoxuan; the above work was obtained through the efforts of Master Xue-tou and others of the Vinaya School.
The aforementioned *vinaya-karman* (monastic procedures) constitutes the hands and feet of the community’s practice;
it is the very life-force of the Buddha-dharma.
Although the rules and regulations of the Vinaya masters were previously prepared,
there are few that are not incomplete.
Is this not indeed a literary work?
Thus, by means of this, one may supplement the deficiencies in the *Śīla* (Precepts) section.
One work in three fascicles, the *Commentary on the Śāstra Explaining the Mahāyāna*, composed by Dharma Master Famin. The above constitutes one work.
This was requested by the Dharma-transmitting Ajāri and others of the Mantra School (Shingon).
The aforementioned *Mahayana-shastra-vyākhyā* is a horizontal commentary on the teachings of Manifestation (Kengyō).
The secret treasury has been kept closed;
although this fundamental treatise had previously arrived,
its placement on either side was not yet determined.
Now, using these commentaries to corroborate the Mahāyāna: *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one volume in four fascicles, composed by Master Daoli of Kaizhong;

*Annotated Explanation of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one volume in three fascicles, composed by Master Daoli of Kaizhong; *Recorded Commentary on the Opening of the Middle Way in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one volume in five fascicles, composed by Chan Master Wenxi; *General Exposition of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one volume in two fascicles, composed by Dharma Master Zhishen; *Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one fascicle, composed by Dharma Master Hanyong; *Sectional Outline for the Commentary on the Opening of the Middle Way in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one fascicle, composed by Master Daoli of Kaizhong; *The Five Teachings and Their Meanings in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, one fascicle, composed by Chan Master Wenxi. The above are the works concerning the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
"Exhausting the subtle and completing the transformations"—
this is a designation for that which is wondrously transcendent.
As for the person who composed this commentary:
The various points of your doctrinal arguments are superficial on both sides;
they are thus obstructed and stymied.
Reaching the time of Kai Zhongli Gong,
the Great Master [Dao’an] cleared away the weeds and vines to reveal the ultimate truth.
Today we see that the true scriptures of the Great Tang have flourished in recent times, with the proliferation of lectures on literature and the exposition of its meanings.
Taking these commentaries as a guide,
he lectured on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* at every monastery to transform and deliver laypeople,
using Master Yi’s commentary as his primary text.
The followers of the black-robed school all say:
"Although there are commentaries and sub-commentaries by masters of the śāstras,"
My humble wisdom is insufficient;
having recently begun to study this text,
the mirror of the Dharma becomes ever clearer.
As for "The Lamp of Wisdom Shining Ever More Brightly":

one volume and two fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary* composed by Dharma Master Kai Zhongdao; two volumes of the *Renwang Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary*; one volume of the *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; and one volume of the *Commentary on the Vajragarbha [Chapter] of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* annotated by Wang Jie of Mount Nanyue. The above are the commentaries and such.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Meaning) and the *Sūkṣmācāra* (Subtle Conduct) were composed in the land of the Jinas;
these commentaries by various masters have flourished extensively in recent times,
all of which treat the works of other teachers as secondary.
Taking these commentaries as authoritative:
since the rise of Buddhism brings about the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it can proclaim the ancient principles to people and entrust the new reality to them;
thus, the fundamental texts of the sutras are not to be altered.
These are merely the essential teachings being transmitted for the sake of the Dharma’s meaning:

one fascicle of the *Essential Method of the Majestic Virtue of the Buddha Sahastraraśmirāja*, one fascicle of the *Essential Method of the Majestic Virtue of the Six Boys*, one fascicle of the *Essential Method of the Majestic Virtue of the Boy Kumbhīra*, and one fascicle of the *Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Great General*. Āḥ.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Great General and Chief Marshal Cunda*, one fascicle;
*The Ritual for the Sequence of Recitation of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Threefold Siddhi Method of Mahāvairocana*, one fascicle;
*The Chinese-Sanskrit Comparative Text of the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Based on the Imperial Edition*, one fascicle; *The Essential Recitation of the Northern King Vaiśravaṇa*.

The *Dharmaparyāya* in two fascicles; the *Vairocanī-devī-adhyeṣaṇā-dharmarakṣa* in one fascicle; the *Sensha-shin-ki* (Record of the Sandha Deity) together with the *Japa-vidhi* (Method for Recitation) in one fascicle;

and the *Bodhirāja-ki* (Record of King Bodhi), including the various *yoga* rituals and initiation manuals (*abhiṣeka-vidhi*) for the deities he received and studied—all these were no different from those previously brought across [to China], so they were not annotated further.
These are the dharma-gates of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.
Whether one has mastered them or not yet mastered them.
Their number is not small;
however, there are only the essential points for the present age.
As for the fundamental principles of the Secret School, they do not essentially differ from the ordinary teachings.
There is one statue of the Buddha King of a Thousand Rays; there are as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and as many particles of dust as there are in the Ganges.
Each receives a distinct title according to their original practices;
only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully comprehend this.
The Buddha of the Thousand Rays of Light mentioned here is the original teacher of Avalokiteśvara;
this matter is perfectly clear.
This image had not been seen before;
therefore, it was requested as detailed above.
One statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of the Water-Moon, intended for the practice of Great Compassion.
Manifesting transformed bodies in myriad directions,
he contemplates sentient beings,
uprooting their suffering and bestowing happiness upon them.
Therefore, he manifested these physical forms to inspire faith in sentient beings.
Now, when people of the Tang Dynasty see them,
they universally regard them as causes for the removal of calamities.
The world regards this as a source of blessings for one's life.
Since such an image has not yet circulated here,
I have requested it as detailed above.

The Great Marshal himself shall provide one set of the mandala consisting of over fifty figures in total: one image of the Great Marshal’s body of great compassion, one image of the Great Marshal’s wrathful body, and one image of the Great Marshal’s emanation body. As for this Great Marshal:
This is the wheel of the Tathāgata’s teaching and command.
For the sake of providing salvation and protection to sentient beings,
the Buddha manifests in the form of a Great General.
The forms of the various false views shall have their heads split into seven pieces;
upon hearing the names of the multitude of evils, the dust of the demonic paths shall scatter.
As the original sutra says:
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are kings, ministers, or others who respectfully pay homage and recite this mantra,
the lands and territories of those individuals [shall be protected]."
There will be no fear of wicked bandits, nor calamities, misfortunes, epidemics, droughts, floods, or unseasonable winds and frosts.
The king’s majesty and virtue will redouble,
and all the people will live in peace and tranquility.
Regarding the passage, "In whatever cities, towns, or villages those who uphold this sutra may dwell,
there shall be none who do not receive its benefits," it is further stated:
If a kingdom is beset by calamity or the rains are irregular,
one should place this mantra of the Great General upon the four city gates.
Thereupon, wind and rain will arrive in their proper seasons;
the kingdom will be pacified, and the neighboring enemies of the four quarters will not give rise to rebellious intentions. Thus it is said.
Thus, if one acts according to the Dharma,
the state will endure long and remain peaceful;
even a woman of the common people will certainly obtain ten inconceivable benefits.
This is the power of the Great Marshal.
Now it is seen that the Tang Dynasty relies entirely upon this as the treasure for governing the state and the essential means for overcoming adversaries.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva King of Sovereign Concentration praised him in verse, saying:
"I have heard the name of the General;
he is the savior from suffering and calamity in the world."
Among all the great deities,
he is extraordinary and without peer;
his various manifested bodies are infinite.
And uprooted the suffering of sentient beings.
Now that I have heard of this past,
the jewel is inconceivable.
This is the Dharma.
It does not circulate widely in our land;
therefore, I have requested this essential ritual manual and its iconographic illustrations.
This incomparable method for pacifying calamities and summoning blessings—who would not take refuge in it?
This is a single statue of the Great Sage, the thousand-armed and thousand-headed Kumbhīra Youth; as for the youth Kumbhīra on the right:
This is an emanation of Śākyamuni.
A sutra states:
"The Buddha was in the Garden of Joy, preaching the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings."
At that time, the heretic Pāpīyān raised various evil obstacles,
causing all sentient beings to undergo great suffering and affliction.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata secretly transformed himself into the youth Kumbhīra.
It subdues non-Buddhists and all māras,
benefiting sentient beings within this degenerate age;
this Dharma is especially a treasure that stabilizes the state and benefits all things.
The marvelous power of the Dharma is inconceivable.
This image, along with its ritual procedures,
is a secret kept by the Vidyādharas.
This has not been seen in our country;
we request that it be brought as specified above.
One statue of the Six Great Holy Child Attendants: regarding these six child attendants on the right—
The Sūtra states:
"They are all emanations of the Buddhas of the past,
manifested for the purpose of protecting and rescuing all sentient beings."
If there is a land where this dharma is practiced,
[the deity] will immediately manifest his body to protect the nation and benefit the people;
this is witnessed today among the people of the Tang Dynasty.
One who cultivates this dharma extensively will perceive its profound power;
such a sacred image has not yet circulated here in this land.
Consequently, he was invited;
however, the ritual procedures for his practice were also extremely sparse and rudimentary.
One statue of the Great Sage Kāpiśī Śakra Devendra; this deity on the right is a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Tathāgata.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Qin Dynasty.
In the past, during the Zhou dynasty, the Five Emperors were moved by divine inspiration, and this deity followed them to escort them.
Now, throughout the Tang realm, this deity is highly esteemed as a powerful means for protecting the state; if those who are ill invoke its name, their ailments are immediately dispelled.
Those who are poor will surely become wealthy through reliance on this vow;
its efficacy has been clearly manifested,
such that there is not a single person who does not take refuge in it.
Now, the Buddha’s transformation of beings flows from the West to the East,
responding to the times and benefiting all things;
how could this not be the untransformed state of the Tathāgata?

One statue of the Son of Heaven of the Three Luminaries and one statue of the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions. Regarding the "Three Luminaries" on the right: these are the sun, moon, and five planets, collectively known as the Seven Radiant Bodies (*saptagraha*).
As for the twenty-eight lunar mansions, comprising seven stars in each of the four directions, the people of this land hear only their names and see only their light.
Its shape and dimensions are unknown;
the form and image of this constellation Jyotiṣka are especially secret and esoteric,
and it truly possesses spiritual efficacy.
Even in the land of Tang, such things are not widely transmitted;
how much more so in the Land of the Rising Sun, where they have never been seen before?
It is merely that the diviners and geomancers have inferred their forms through conjecture.
It is because the transmitted models were not in accord with the truth.
Now, the images requested each have their own standard for representation.
Among them, there is one statue of the Holy Bodhivṛkṣarāja; on its right is Bodhivṛkṣarāja.
He was a mountain deity of Mount Daitang.

There was a bhikṣu on Mount Lou in Runzhou who, while practicing and refining his meditative discipline, had a vision of this deity manifesting its form to display its spiritual power. Because the deity received the precepts and cultivated the Way [under him], it was named King Bodhi.
In accordance with people's prayers for protection and the fulfillment of their vows, he subsequently became a guardian of the state and people flocked to him.
Consequently, images were created everywhere and everyone held them in high esteem; having personally witnessed these events, they are truly worthy of emulation.
One statue of the Sandalwood (Shensha) King, right side; produced during the Tang Dynasty when the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, having traveled far across the Five Indias, was moved by this deity.
This is an emanation of the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
Nowadays, the people of the Tang universally revere this deity for its efficacy in averting disasters and bringing benefit;
its manifestations are evident before our eyes,
such that there is not a single person who does not rely upon its practice.
The households within the temple precincts all rely upon this deity.
Having personally witnessed its spiritual efficacy, it is truly inconceivable.
The full account is as recorded in the inscription.
The items requested are as follows:
one statue of a Bodhisattva and fifteen types of *homa* hearth altars. The aforementioned statue was manifested during the Tang Dynasty;
its spiritual efficacy is profound.
When people raise [this practice], they return [to their original state].
For pacifying calamities and increasing blessings, there is nothing superior to this.
The details are as recorded in the text.
I have requested the items listed herein.
Now, the Ultimate Way is wordless;
yet it cannot be manifested without words.
The ultimate reality transcends form;
it is through the mediation of form that one awakens to it.
That which transcends form is the Three Jewels of True Suchness.
To manifest form is to sustain the Three Jewels.
The Tathāgata’s original vow accords with the capacities of beings by transforming his appearance;
the Great Sage, out of compassion, responds to the times to deliver all things.
The Sūtra says:
"To those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body,
he manifests a Buddha-body."
Even unto those among the eight classes of beings who are to be delivered,
he manifests himself to all and preaches the Dharma for them;
such is the case during the era of the True Dharma.
The retinue of Māra lacks majesty;
therefore, the Buddha’s transformation [teachings] dwell largely in compassion during the age of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma.
Evil influences arise in competition;
for this reason, the Tathāgata manifests many forms of wrathful fury.
Such is the power of the Buddha;
it is truly a treasure that stabilizes the nation and benefits all people.
Receive and uphold it with the highest reverence.
Its benefits are boundless:
externally it crushes the armies of Māra;
internally it subdues the afflictions.
The wisdom and compassion of the Buddhas are thus.

The articles for the Dharma-transmitting Ācārya (Dharmadeśaka-ācārya): one five-pronged golden vajra, one three-pronged vajra, one set of copper cymbals, one copper gong, one string of rudrākṣa beads, one volume of the Tārā Sanskrit manuscript, one face of the thirty-seven-deity seed-syllable maṇḍala of Vajrasamudra, seventeen types of Indian offerings including one white cotton cloth and one Indian sandalwood mat. The two scrolls of the *Dharmadeśaka-ācārya-śiṣyābhiṣeka-vidhi* (The Ritual for Bestowing Initiation upon Disciples by the Dharma-transmitting Ācārya). The above are the ritual implements.
These were transmitted by the Acharya of Sōji-ji Temple.
Jōkō departed in the middle month of summer in the fifth year of the Shōwa era,
accompanying Kanemaro Sugawara no Shinnō, who was serving as an envoy to Tang China.
As mentioned above, the fourth ship departed for Śīna.
In the sixth month of that year, it reached the shore at Yangzhou.
In the latter part of the eighth month, it arrived at the Grand Commandery of Huainan and was stationed at the Guanglin Hall.
In the twelfth month of the same year, he resided at the Daibi Jinian Yuan (Hall of Great Compassionate Recitation) of Xiling Temple.
He accompanied the Abbot Wenxu, the Consecration Ācārya of that temple,
as well as the Dharma Master Yuanzhao, a Great Virtuous One who expounded the Three Teachings at Hualin Temple.
He practiced both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings concurrently.
On the fourth day of the first month of the sixth year, he prepared a vegetarian feast for two hundred monks,
making offerings to the fourfold assembly.
On this day, the virtuous elders and administrators of all the monasteries attended the meal assembly to partake in the offerings with sympathetic joy.
During the night, Changxiao went to his teacher’s side to receive instruction in Yoga;
during the day, he traveled throughout the various monasteries to seek out and inquire about the Dharma gates.
Thereupon, he summoned the attendant Li Quan and others to paint images of the Great General and the various deities of the mandala,
as well as to transcribe the written documents;
these matters gradually proceeded in orderly succession.
On the nineteenth day of the second month, he received the consecration for the rank of Dharma-transmitting Ācārya.
On this day, a great vegetarian feast was prepared to provide universal offerings to the assembly.
The official Fujiwara no Tadamoto was appointed as the administrator to remain behind.
The invited Dan-chi (True Hall) practitioners— Gao Zhuzhi, Cheng An-chi, Su-de, Liang Dong,
and others— together attended the ritual site to cast flowers and determine the principal deity.
He received the empowerment of the five wisdoms.
On the twenty-first day, in accordance with an imperial decree, he departed from Lizhou and returned to the capital.
Changxiao’s original field of study was the branch of the Three Treatises (Sanlun).
Furthermore, regarding the section on mantras,
his talent was not heard of and his words were not worth taking up.
Those who encounter their time are admitted into the training hall and limited to a term of thirty years;
yet, seeking through the One Vehicle,
the task is heavy while human capacity is weak.
Day and night he was diligent and earnest.
Although the interests of the state were difficult to reconcile with the neglect of his kin at ten thousand *li* away, and his mind remained fixed upon distant realms,
he nevertheless studied both the Exoteric and Esoteric paths extensively.
Before I had seen [the Emperor] and fully understood it, an imperial decree was issued prohibiting my continued stay;
consequently, I returned with the envoys.
Shortly thereafter, the ritual protocols for this dharma were completed as detailed in the following items.
On the fifth day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Jōwa era,
submitted by the śramaṇa Chōkō, Dharma Master of the Great Dharma Transmission, who has entered Tang to study the Dharma.
